alignment.note: Greek opens with paratactic Καί and Latin matches with Et; the Peshitta lacks an initial conjunction here, instead deferring its connective particle ܕܝܢ ('but/now') to second position, a normal Syriac discourse-ordering.
ἦσαν / erant; the Peshitta expresses the periphrastic past with the enclitic ܗܘܘ later in the clause (token 5).

The Syriac postpositive particle ܕܝܢ ('but/now') has no direct counterpart in the Greek or Latin of this clause; it supplies the connective force that Greek/Latin place at the head with Καί/Et, reflecting a syntactic restructuring rather than a semantic difference.
Ἰωάννου / ܕܝܘܚܢܢ / Joannis.

Greek attaches a second article cluster (οἱ τῶν Φαρισαῖοι) co-ordinating 'the [disciples] of the Pharisees,' while the Peshitta compresses this to the single conjoined noun ܘܦܪܝܫܐ ('and the Pharisees') and the Vulgate to et pharisæi; in the latter two 'the disciples of' is left implicit and the Pharisees appear as bare subjects of the participle.

Greek uses a single present participle νηστεύοντες ('fasting') and Latin the participle jejunantes; the Peshitta renders the durative idea with a periphrastic construction, finite participle ܨܝܡܝܢ plus enclitic perfect ܗܘܘ ('were fasting'), a characteristically Syriac analytic past.
Greek connects with simple καί; the Vulgate inserts a colon before resuming et veniunt, segmenting the verse into two cola, a punctuational rather than lexical divergence.
ἔρχονται / ܘܐܬܘ / veniunt; the Peshitta carries its 'and' prefixed (ܘ) to the verb.
Connective καί / et linking the two finite verbs; in the Peshitta this conjunction is again prefixed to the following verb.
λέγουσιν / ܘܐܡܪܝܢ / dicunt.

All three attest the dative/prepositional pronoun (αὐτῷ / ܠܗ / illi); the Vulgate additionally places a colon introducing direct speech, which the Greek marks with a high point and the Syriac leaves unpunctuated.
Greek uses the two-word interrogative phrase διὰ τί ('on account of what / why'); the Peshitta ܠܡܢܐ and Latin Quare each render it with a single interrogative word, semantically equivalent.
οἱ μαθηταί / ܬܠܡܝܕܘܗܝ / discipuli; note the Syriac noun bears a possessive suffix ('his disciples'), but in context functions appositionally to John.
Ἰωάννου / ܕܝܘܚܢܢ / Joannis.

Greek fully repeats the article + noun phrase (καὶ οἱ μαθηταὶ τῶν Φαρισαίων, 'and the disciples of the Pharisees'); the Peshitta compresses to a single conjoined genitive ܘܕܦܪܝܫܐ and the Vulgate to et pharisæorum, both leaving 'disciples' implicit by ellipsis from the parallel clause.
νηστεύουσιν / ܨܝܡܝܢ / jejunant ('they fast').
The adversative δέ / autem marking the contrast 'but your disciples'; the Peshitta does not render a separate adversative particle here, relying on the contrastive emphasis carried by ܕܝܠܟ.

Greek expresses possession with the possessive adjective σοί preceding μαθηταί ('your disciples'); the Peshitta doubles the possession, suffixing the pronoun to the noun ܘܬܠܡܝܕܝܟ and reinforcing it with the independent emphatic genitive ܕܝܠܟ ('yours'), a typical Syriac intensifier; the Vulgate uses the simple possessive tui.
Negative particle οὐ / ܠܐ / non.
Closing verb νηστεύουσιν / ܨܝܡܝܢ / jejunant with interrogative punctuation; the Greek further marks a paragraph break (¶) absent from the other witnesses.
